vignette:
Imani’s hands tell the story of a life lived in the soil. The palms are tough as cured leather, the knuckles swollen, and the lines etched into her skin are permanently filled with the dark, rich earth of the shamba. At seventy-four, she still finds a deep, rhythmic comfort in her work—the pull of a stubborn weed, the weight of a water-filled gourd, the particular scent of tomato leaves in the hot afternoon sun. For most of her life, this work was her sanctuary. Now, it has become a place of ambush.

The trouble, she explains, began when she was nineteen. She speaks of it in a quiet, steady voice, as if recounting a story that happened to someone else. It was the end of the harvest season, the air thick with the smell of maize dust and coming rain. She was walking home from a neighboring farm, taking a familiar shortcut along the riverbank as dusk settled. The memory isn’t a clear narrative but a collection of sharp, sensory fragments: the scratch of a burlap sack against her cheek, the overwhelming scent of wild basil crushed underfoot, the chilling realization that the footsteps behind her were quickening. He was a stranger, a man who had been working the harvest for a few weeks. She remembers the weight of him, the way the damp earth pressed into her back, and the sound of the river rushing nearby, indifferent.

When it was over, she walked home in the dark, washed herself with cold water from the basin outside, and never spoke a word of it to anyone. To speak of it would have been to make it real, to invite a shame she felt was hers alone to carry. So she folded the memory into a small, hard knot and buried it deep within herself. Her life continued. She worked the land, married a man from her village, raised two children, and eventually buried her husband. Through it all, the knot remained, untouched.

For fifty years, she managed. The work helped; the sheer physical exhaustion it brought was a balm, leaving no room for thoughts to wander at night. But there were rules she created for herself without ever naming them. She never walked alone at dusk. The smell of rain on dry soil could make her stomach clench for reasons she refused to examine. She would startle violently if a man, even her own husband, came up behind her too quietly in the fields. She dismissed it all as being "jumpy."

It wasn't until David came into her life two years ago that the knot began to unravel. He is a kind man, a retired teacher with soft hands and a gentle voice. He loves the garden she tends, and he loves her. But his kindness is a key turning a lock she had long forgotten. When he reaches to brush a stray leaf from her hair, she flinches. When he embraces her from behind while she washes vegetables at the sink, her body goes rigid, her breath catching in her throat. The scent of his aftershave, clean and herbal, sometimes mixes in her mind with the memory of crushed basil, and she has to push him away, a wave of nausea and inexplicable rage rising in her.

The nights are the worst. She lies awake next to this good, sleeping man, her heart pounding a frantic rhythm against her ribs. Every creak of the house is an intruder. A shadow shifting in the moonlight is a figure by the door. She often gets up and sits in the kitchen until dawn, watching the sun rise over the fields that have held her secrets for a lifetime. The land that once offered her solace now feels like a silent witness to a crime she was forced to endure, its soil holding memories she can no longer bury.
